claims.text: The starting material is nanocrystalline W38Ta36Cr15V11.
SPS can be used to consolidate refractory-alloy powders into fine-grained bulk material.
SPS at approximately 1200°C for 5 minutes under vacuum is suitable for consolidating W38Ta36Cr15V11.
A post-SPS anneal at approximately 800°C for 10 minutes will induce controlled grain growth.
The combined SPS and annealing treatment changes the alloy from nanocrystalline to ultrafine-grained.
The combined treatment reduces the density of high-angle grain boundaries.
Mild grain growth lowers the overall grain-boundary energy.
Reducing grain-boundary density reduces the number of nucleation sites for Cr/V-rich precipitates.
The SPS-and-anneal treatment enhances irradiation-defect sink efficiency.
The proposed microstructural stabilization prevents the formation and growth of radiation-induced precipitates.
At approximately 8 dpa and 400–500°C, the treatment will reduce precipitate density by more than 50% relative to unmodified nanocrystalline W38Ta36Cr15V11.
At approximately 8 dpa and 400–500°C, the treated alloy will retain negligible irradiation hardening.
Unmodified nanocrystalline W38Ta36Cr15V11 develops radiation-induced Cr/V-rich precipitates.
Radiation-induced Cr/V-rich precipitates in the unmodified alloy can cause localized hardening.
SPS improves the suitability of refractory alloys for practical bulk fabrication through rapid consolidation and controlled fine-grained structure.
The hypothesis is limited to irradiation temperatures of 400–500°C and doses up to approximately 8 dpa.
The range 400–500°C is fusion-relevant for the proposed irradiation test.

contradictions.description: The hypothesis and mechanism use prevention language, implying essentially no radiation-induced precipitation, whereas the predicted and falsification criteria require only a greater-than-50% reduction, which permits substantial residual precipitation.
